video.title: How machines learn from examples
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher, Kenya (main character)
Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

chapters.label: A scam in the staff group

scenes.visual: Staff room, morning light. Close-up of Joseph’s phone: a group-chat message slides in — “Your salary is on hold — confirm your bank details today.” He switches to his text messages: a similar text sits under a warning banner, ‘Suspected spam’. Cut to Joseph’s face: eyebrows up, curious half-smile.
scenes.animation: Message bubble slides up with a 150 ms bounce; warning banner pops in (≤ 200 ms). Quick push-in on Joseph’s face.
scenes.narration: A scam in our staff group — and my phone already flagged one just like it as spam. How did it learn to do that?
scenes.sound: Phone buzz; light music bed starts.
scenes.vids: Flat phone illustration; put the message text in Vids text boxes so it can be translated. No app logos. Character: Joseph, illustrated teacher with ink outlines.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the lesson title and a yellow ‘AI’ track chip with the spark icon.
scenes.animation: Mark scales 0→100% with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: how machines learn from examples — step by step.
scenes.vids: Use the Darsi title template (see brand kit). Keep the chip as icon + word.

scenes.visual: A big pile of wordless message cards (just lines) slides in. Many hands — young and old, different skin tones — pick up cards and clip a tag on each: a tag with a warning triangle (spam) or a tag with a plain envelope (not spam). The tagged cards stack into two neat piles.
scenes.animation: Cards fly in on curved paths (2 s); tags clip on, 150 ms each; the two piles grow.
scenes.narration: It starts with people. They collect examples — for a spam filter, lots of emails — and give each one a label, the right answer: spam, or not spam. These labelled examples are the training data.
scenes.sound: Soft paper shuffles; a light click for each tag.
scenes.vids: Keep the cards wordless so the scene works in every language. Tags use Darsi icons (warning, mail), not words.

scenes.visual: Both piles feed into a big cog. As it turns, the same small icons light up again and again on the spam cards — a key (PIN), a clock (‘today’), a link. Sparkles mark each repeat. Out of the cog drops a small box with a sparkle on it: the model.
scenes.animation: Cog turns steadily; repeated icons pulse once each (≤ 200 ms); the model box drops out with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Next, training. The computer searches the labelled examples for patterns — like words and requests that keep appearing in spam: “confirm your PIN”, “act today”. What it finds is stored as a model: patterns kept as numbers.
scenes.sound: Gentle machine whirr; a soft ping as the model drops out.
scenes.vids: Show the model as a simple box, never a brain or a robot. Icons from the Darsi set; rotate the cog with a Vids animation.

scenes.visual: A few cards that sat aside in a closed box now go to the model one at a time. The model clips a tag on each; the real tag is shown beside it. Most match (check badge), one doesn’t (cross badge). Then new, different-looking cards join the piles and the cog turns again.
scenes.animation: Cards slide in one by one; check and cross badges pop (150 ms). Quick loop arrow back to the cog.
scenes.narration: Then we test the model on labelled examples it has never seen, and check its guesses against the real labels. Too many wrong? People add more examples — and more varied ones — and train it again.
scenes.sound: Soft tick for each match; low blip for the miss.
scenes.vids: Matches: blue badge with a check icon. Miss: cross icon. Colour is never the only signal.

scenes.visual: Clean white card with the AI track chip. The five-step row builds left to right, joined by arrows: boxes (collect examples), tag (label them), cog (train: find patterns), check-square (test on new examples), sparkle (use: make predictions). The last step is filled with the AI track colour.
scenes.animation: Steps appear one by one, 300 ms apart, with arrows drawing between them.
scenes.narration: So, machine learning is a way of building AI where the computer finds patterns in examples, instead of a person writing every rule. Five steps: collect examples, label them, train, test — then use the model to make predictions.
scenes.vids: Build all five steps from the ml-pipeline diagram (the starter slide shows four icons). Hold the full row for at least 6 seconds so teachers can read it in a second language.

scenes.visual: A school garden under a mango tree. Joseph and a younger pupil kneel by a basket. Joseph holds up mangoes one by one; a small ripe or not-ripe icon pops above each. The pupil sorts a few; Joseph gently swaps one back. Then a new basket arrives and the pupil sorts it alone, smiling.
scenes.animation: Icons pop above each mango (150 ms). Wipe to the new basket; the pupil’s sorting is quick and simple.
scenes.narration: It’s like teaching a younger pupil to pick ripe mangoes. You show many mangoes and say “ripe” or “not ripe”. They notice patterns — colour, softness, smell — and you correct their mistakes. Then you test them with mangoes they’ve never seen.
scenes.sound: Birdsong and a light breeze for 2 s.
scenes.vids: Mangoes: flat shapes from green to yellow-orange. Use icons, not words, for ripe and not ripe. Illustrated pupil in a local school uniform.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma pops in beside the five-step row, one eyebrow raised, chalk in hand. Three answer cards drop in below her.
scenes.animation: Character slides in from the side; answer cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Why do we test a model on examples it has never seen?
scenes.sound: Three gentle ‘pop’ sounds for the cards.
scenes.vids: The app pauses here (diamond marker). For the MP4 shared outside the app, hold this frame for 3 seconds with a small countdown ring.

scenes.visual: The card ‘To check it learned patterns’ gets a blue check badge. Split screen below: on the left, a clipboard list of blocked numbers lets a new scam card slip past; on the right, the model box catches the same card with a warning tag.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms). Quick 0.8 s confetti of three shapes in kola, sunbird and ink.
scenes.narration: To check it learned patterns, not just its examples. A list of blocked numbers only stops numbers someone added. A model that learned patterns can often catch a new scam it has never seen.
scenes.vids: Use blue for correct (never green) and always pair it with the check icon. Show phone numbers as dots and dashes, never real numbers.

scenes.visual: Three cards, about 7 seconds each: a farmer’s phone over a cassava leaf, with a stack of leaf photos and expert tags behind it; a teacher speaking into a phone, with sound waves from many speakers behind; a river map with gauge pins feeding a model box that shows an alert badge.
scenes.animation: Each card flips in from the right. Keep motion simple and readable on a small screen.
scenes.narration: You’ll find these steps in many tools. One cassava app was trained on thousands of leaf photos, each labelled by experts. One voice-typing tool learned from recordings of native speakers. And one flood-forecasting system learned from records of thousands of river gauges.
scenes.vids: Use flat icons from the Darsi set on white cards. Do not show real app logos or brand names on screen.

scenes.visual: A phone screen with two buckets, ‘Safe message’ and ‘Scam’, each holding a few message cards. A finger types a new message into a test box; a guess appears with a short confidence bar.
scenes.animation: Cards drop into the buckets (150 ms each); the confidence bar fills left to right in 1 s.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: train a scam spotter
scenes.narration: In the app, after this video, you’ll train a tiny scam spotter: give it messages labelled safe or scam, then test it on one it has never seen.
scenes.sound: Soft click as each card lands.
scenes.vids: Screen-record the TrainClassifier lab in the app, or mock it up with flat shapes. Bucket labels go in text boxes so they can be translated.

scenes.visual: Joseph holds up his phone: a new text with the ‘suspected spam’ banner. Two answer cards appear beside him.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. My phone marks a new text as “suspected spam”. Is that a prediction?
scenes.vids: Second diamond marker — the app pauses for the question. In the MP4, hold for 3 seconds, then highlight ‘Yes — a best guess about now’.

scenes.visual: The ‘Yes’ card gets the check badge, then the screen resolves into three summary cards: a stack of tagged cards (labelled examples), a cog beside a check-square (train and test), a sparkle with a question mark (predictions).
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.on_screen_text: Labelled examples · Train and test · Predictions
scenes.narration: Yes — “Is this spam?” is a prediction about now. Remember: collect and label examples, train a model, test it on new ones, then use it to make predictions. And many models stay the same until people retrain them.
scenes.vids: Hold the three cards for 5 seconds.

scenes.visual: Joseph’s classroom. The board has two chalk columns: triangles of many sizes on the left; squares, circles and stars on the right. Pupils hold up one or two fingers to predict new shapes; Joseph reveals the secret. End card: Darsi mark and ‘Next: Good data, fair AI’.
scenes.animation: New shapes appear on the board one by one; fingers go up. End card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: play “Be the machine”. Draw shapes that are zogs and shapes that are not. Pupils find the hidden pattern, then predict new shapes — the same steps a spam filter follows.
scenes.sound: Music resolves; no end jingle longer than 1 s.
scenes.vids: Classroom: illustrated pupils in local school uniforms; avoid stereotyped imagery. End card from the Darsi template.

checkpoints.prompt: Why do we test a model on examples it has never seen?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — new examples show whether it learned patterns that work beyond the examples it trained on.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the test uses examples it has never seen, to check it learned patterns rather than memorised its examples.

checkpoints.prompt: Joseph’s phone marks a new text as “suspected spam”. Is that a prediction?

options.text: Yes — a best guess about now
No — it isn’t about the future

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a prediction is a best guess about something unknown. “Is this spam?” is about now.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — predictions don’t have to be about the future. “Is this spam?” is a best guess about now.

video.vids_prompt: Create a 3 minute 47 second animated explainer video for teachers titled “How machines learn from examples”. Style: flat, friendly illustration with bold ink outlines, light grey backgrounds, a tangerine (#ff6a2b) brand colour and a sunny yellow (#ffc53d) accent; no gradients or blur. Main character: Joseph, a computer studies teacher in Kenya; cameo: Salma, a maths teacher. Follow the attached script scene by scene: a phone flags a scam text; people collect and label example messages; training finds patterns and builds a model; testing on new examples; the five steps; teaching a pupil to pick ripe mangoes; real examples (cassava photos, voice typing, flood forecasts); a scam-spotter lab preview; two quick quiz pauses; end with a classroom game. Use the narration exactly as written, a warm, calm voice, and keep on-screen text to six words or fewer per scene.
